ādhi
(‘illness of the मिन्द्’)
------------------------------------------
The ancient Hindu sages have recognised that the body and the मिन्द् form one unit and that this unit is of fundamental importance in achieving anything worthwhile in life. Hence each should be kept in a healthy condition and in harmony with the other. व्याधि (illness of the body) and आधि (illness of the मिन्द्) are both considered to be serious obstacles in the path of progress, whether temporal or spiritual.
In most general terms, anything that disturbs the equilibrium of the body is a व्याधि and anything that upsets the equi-poise of the मिन्द् is an आधि. The ariṣaḍ-vargas or six enemies viz., lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride and envy, as also worries and anxieties are examples of आधि. राग (attachment) and द्वेष (aversion) are the root causes of all ādhis. Conquest of these will help in removing the ādhis.
In the धर्मशास्त्रस्, the word is used in the sense of a pledge, deposit or article of mortgage.

Adhikāra Nandi
------------------------------------------
Everyone that enters a शिव temple cannot fail to see the image of नन्दि, the reclining bull. In इचोनोग्रफ्य्, नन्दि or Nandikeśvara is depicted in two forms as vṛṣabha or reclining bull and as अधिकार नन्दि, an image resembling that of शिव. In this aspect , the two back hands hold the परशु (battle axe) and the mṛga (antelope) and the two front hands are folded on the chest in the añjali (obeisance) pose. In all other respects, the characte-ristics of the image are identical with those of शिव.
Since he is the chief of the gaṇas (retinues) of शिव, exercising his authority (adhikāra) over them, he is christened ‘Adhikāra नन्दि.’ He is also called Nandīśvara or Nandikeśvara.
As regards the origin of this deity, there are three different accounts available in Hindu म्य्थोलोग्य्. Desirous of a son, a sage Sālaṅkāyana by name, propitiated विष्णु, who granted his wish by producing a boy exactly resembling शिव, from the right side of his body. He was named Nandikeśvara. According to another account, a sage called नन्दि obtained the status of a god and the headship of the gaṇas of शिव by propitiating him. A third account depicts him as emerging from the yāgaśālā (sacrificial shed) of the blind sage Śilāda, in the form of an young lad resembling शिव, thus bringing ‘nandi’ or joy to him. Śilāda adopted him as his son.
Adhikāra नन्दि took a prominent part in the destruction of दक्ष’s sacrifice.
He is more often represented as a bull and also described as the वाहन (mount) of शिव.
See also NANDI.

adhikamāsa
(‘intercalary month’)
------------------------------------------
From the most ancient times, all religious activity of the Hindus was performed at times considered auspicious or suitable for them. Calculations were done based on the movements of the sun, the मोओन्, the प्लनेत्स् and the स्तर्स्. This resulted in the growth of an entire science of Vedic अस्त्रोनोम्य्, ‘Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa’.
The most fundamental periods of time, common to all the nations are the day, the month and the year. The day is due to the revolution of the earth round its axis. The month is mainly a lunar phenomenon based on the waxing and waning of the मोओन्. The year is due to the apparent motion of the sun as seen from the earth. Hence the Hindus followed a luni-solar चलेन्दर् from the ancient times, and being aware of the difference between the two ways of calculating, also provided for the necessary adjustments to be made to bring the two into consonance. The lunar year on which are based the religious activities, is less than the solar year by about eleven days. Hence two intercalary months are added in five years, one being a second आषाढ (the 4th lunar month) at the end of 2 years and a second pauṣa (the 10th lunar month) at the end of another 2 years. This is according to Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa. Later works give varying periods after which the इन्तेर्चलर्य् मोन्थ् occurs. The general rule seems to be that the lunar month in which no सङ्क्रान्ति (apparent movement of the sun from one constellation to the next, as seen from the earth) occurs, is called an अधिकमास and bears the same name of the next lunar month which is called śuddha or nija or prākṛta, to distinguish it from the former.
Somehow, the अधिकमास was considered even from the ancient times, inauspicious and hence named मलमास (‘the dirty month’), malimluca (‘a thief’), अṁहस्पति (‘the lord of sins’) and so on. During this month one was advised to avoid acts like consecrating Vedic fires, installing images, offering gifts, observing vratas or religious vows, performing उपनयन and other सṁस्कारस् (puri-ficatory rites).
However in some पुराणस् like the Padma (6.64) the इन्तेर्चलर्य् मोन्थ् is named ‘puruṣottama-māsa’ (‘month of Lord विष्णु’), probably with a view to reducing the opprobrium attached to it and considered, on the other hand, as holy.

adhikāra
(‘competence’)
------------------------------------------
All people are not endowed with equal ability. To perform an act properly and efficiently one must have at least the minimum capacity and competence in that field. Training can improve it but cannot create it. This patent fact has been recognised by the Hindu scriptures and propagated under the nomenclature ‘adhikāra.’ For instance, it is the man who is endowed with physical strength and mental courage that has the अधिकार for joining the armed forces. Similarly it is the person who is endowed with more than average intelligence, a fair degree of scholarship and a capacity to speak well, that has the अधिकार to enter the teaching profession. Again, it is the person who has practised at least to a certain degree, purity and self-control, that has the अधिकार to become a monk.
In most cases, अधिकार can be developed by assiduous cultivation. One who has अधिकार is called an ‘adhikārin’ and the doctrine that advocates the need for अधिकार is called ‘adhikāravāda.’ The differences among the adhikārins are termed ‘adhikāribheda.’
In this च्रेअतिओन् there is nothing that is absolute. Everything is relative. Divergences and differences do exist. The ‘Doctrine of अधिकार or Adhikārabheda’ is just a recognition of this patent fact. It does not necessarily suggest a gradation, with its corollary of ‘higher’ and ‘lower’ status, implying pride or contempt. It is more an acceptance of a fact as it exists, helping one to understand where one stands and start one’s progress from that base. Also it is designed to awaken one to one’s duties rather than to one’s rights and privileges.

ādhibhautika
------------------------------------------
The three words respectively mean: pertaining to
the भूत or living beings;
the दैव or fate, unseen forces and gods;
the ātma or the body (and the मिन्द्).
Sorrow and suffering (duḥkha, tāpa) are inevitable in life. In fact, they are a part of life. A knowledge of their origin, causes and even categorisation helps one to minimise their effect if not eradicate them. The Hindu religious works usually call them ‘tāpatraya,’ ‘the three miseries.’ They are: आध्यात्मिक, आधिदैविक and आधिभौतिक.
The आध्यात्मिक दुःख or tāpa is that which is caused by bodily suffering and mental anguish. Hereditary diseases like leprosy, disabilities like blindness or lameness and diseases caused by the violation of the rules of health and sanitation are classed under this. The mental agony caused by worries and anxieties, attachment and aversion, also comes under this group.
The आधिदैविक duḥka or tāpa is that which is caused by दैव. The word दैव includes the power of time, nature and the unseen hand or fate. Diseases caused by the changing seasons, misery caused by the elemental forces like floods and fire, suffering caused by black magic or disembodied spirits or gods who are displeased, natural tribulations due to hunger, thirst and old-age belong to this group.
The आधिभौतिक दुःख or tāpa is that which is caused by other bhūtas or living beings, like wild animals, snakes, or enemies.
Some of these, like hereditary diseases or physical disabilities cannot be got rid of. Hence they must be endured. Some like the diseases caused by change of seasons or the machinations of enemies can be countered by taking appropriate precautions. However, raising the मिन्द् to the level of the spirit, thus transcending the limitations imposed by the body-मिन्द् complex, is the best solution to offset the effects of tāpatraya.

adhikaraṇa
(‘ground or support’)
------------------------------------------
The word is generally used in the sense of a base, ground or support. For instance, when we say, ‘This is a blue lotus with a sweet smell,’ the lotus flower forms the ‘adhikaraṇa’ for the blue colour as also the sweet smell.
In the Mīmāṁsā philosophy, it is used as a technical term and indicates the section of a work dealing with a particular topic. It consists of five parts: viṣaya (subject of discussion), viśaya or सṁशय (doubt), पूर्वपक्ष (prima facie view), uttara (answer) and सिद्धान्त or nirṇaya (final conclusion).

adhivāsa
(‘to live in’)
------------------------------------------
Temples form a very important part of the Hindu religious institutions and culture. Building of temples has developed, over the years, into a great art. Architecture and इचोनोग्रफ्य् have grown both vast and deep because of it. The images, though prepared strictly according to the standards of इचोनोग्रफ्य्, are unfit to be installed in them unless sanctified ceremonially by rites recommended in the आगमस् (a class of religious works connected with temple worship). ‘Adhivāsa’ is such a rite, making the image ‘live in’ various substances like water and grains. The adhivāsas are three: जलाधिवास, धान्याधिवास and शय्याधिवास. The first is to remedy the effects of chiselling, the second for purifying the physical image and the last for inducing spiritual effulgence.
In जलाधिवास (‘living in water’), the image is taken in a procession round the village, placed on level ground on the bank of a river or tank, sprinkled with the water of the same, wound round with कुश grass and new cloth and ceremonially immersed in the water so that the head lies towards the east and mouth upwards. The duration of जलाधिवास is from one night to nine nights, though three nights are more common. After taking it out of water, the image has to undergo physical and ceremonial cleansing once again.
Dhānyādhivāsa (‘living in grains’) and शय्याधिवास (‘living in the bed’) are actually one ritual in practice. On the वेदि (special platform) a स्थण्डिल (an esoteric geometric design) is inscribed. Grains like wheat, rice, barley and black sesame are spread and a lotus of eight petals is inscribed on the grains. A bed is now prepared over this with five materials viz., wooden plank, skin of deer or tiger, a rug of animal hair, feathers of birds and cloth. In the absence of the first four materials, five layers of cloth can be used. The image is now made to lie for three nights on this bed, with कुश grass underneath it, the head being towards the east and mouth upwards.
The word ‘adhivāsa’ is also used in the sense of ‘perfuming’ or sanctifying with perfumes or other approved materials, any object or objects used in ceremonial worship.
See also PRATIṢṬHĀVIDHI.

adhiṣṭhāna
(‘base, support, substratum’)
------------------------------------------
While discussing the theory of illusory perception, this word is often used in Vedānta to denote the substratum wherein the इल्लुसिओन् occurs. For instance, when a snake is perceived in a rope, or silver in nacre, the rope or the nacre forms the ‘adhiṣṭhāna’ or substratum, for this illusory perception. इग्नोरन्चे of this अधिष्ठान causes the इल्लुसिओन् and its true knowledge dispels it.
While enumerating the five causes responsible for the accomplishment of every action, the Bhagavadgītā (18.14) puts ‘adhiṣṭhāna’ as the first in the list. The word is interpreted there as the body, since the body is the primary basis necessary for all actions.
In works on Hindu Architecture including Temple Architecture, the word denotes the basement of a building or even a column. Innumerable varieties of the same are detailed in those works.
In Civics, the word was used to indicate a seat of administration like a city-council.

adhiṣavaṇa
(‘to press out’)
------------------------------------------
The Vedic sages were fond of performing sacrifices to propitiate the various deities like इन्द्र through whom they could fulfil their wishes. In one group of such sacrifices called Somayāgas, the libation of the juice of the सोम creeper was the most important ceremony. The act of pressing out the juice from the creeper was no less important and even that had a ritualistic bearing. The word ‘adhiṣavaṇa’ is used to indicate both this act of pressing the सोम creeper and the wooden contrivance used in the process. More often, the latter which is in the form of a pair of semicircular wooden boards, is called ‘adhiṣavaṇa-phalaka.’
